claim: SWR1 is a conserved yeast chromatin remodeler that performs histone exchange on +1 nucleosomes adjacent to a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) at gene promoters.
source: SWR1, a conserved yeast chromatin remodeler that performs histone exchange on +1 nucleosomes adjacent to a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) at gene promoters
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established characteristic of SWR1, supported by the broader literature context provided in the introduction.

claim: SWR1 has a kinetic binding preference for DNA of NDR length as opposed to gene-body linker length DNA.
source: We demonstrate that SWR1 has a kinetic binding preference for DNA of NDR length as opposed to gene-body linker length DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing binding kinetics measurements presented in Figure 1C-G and described in the Results section.

claim: SWR1 diffuses on DNA as observed using single and dual color single-particle tracking on DNA stretched with optical tweezers.
source: Using single and dual color single-particle tracking on DNA stretched with optical tweezers, we directly observe SWR1 diffusion on DNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3, with direct observation of SWR1 movement on DNA.

claim: ATP promotes SWR1 diffusion through nucleotide binding rather than ATP hydrolysis.
source: We found that various factors impact SWR1 scanning, including ATP which promotes diffusion through nucleotide binding rather than ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing ATP and ATPγS (non-hydrolyzable analog) effects on diffusion shown in Figure 3.

claim: Swc2, a DNA-binding subunit, plays an important role in the overall diffusive behavior of the SWR1 complex.
source: A DNA-binding subunit, Swc2, plays an important role in the overall diffusive behavior of the complex, as the subunit in isolation retains similar, although faster, scanning properties as the whole remodeler.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing Swc2 DBD diffusion on DNA presented in Figure 4.

claim: ATP-bound SWR1 slides until it encounters a protein roadblock such as dCas9 and nucleosomes.
source: ATP-bound SWR1 slides until it encounters a protein roadblock, of which we tested dCas9 and nucleosomes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing SWR1 diffusion being blocked by dCas9 (Figure 5) and nucleosomes (Figure 6).

claim: The median diffusion coefficient of SWR1 is 0.024 μm²/s in the regime of helical sliding.
source: The median diffusion coefficient, 0.024 μm 2 /s, in the regime of helical sliding
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: SWR1's diffusion coefficient would mediate rapid encounter of NDR-flanking nucleosomes at length scales found in cellular chromatin.
source: The median diffusion coefficient, 0.024 μm 2 /s, in the regime of helical sliding, would mediate rapid encounter of NDR-flanking nucleosomes at length scales found in cellular chromatin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured diffusion coefficient and calculated scanning time (93 ms for 150 bp NDR).

claim: Nucleosome-depleted regions (NDRs) of about 140 bp in length are flanked by two well-positioned nucleosomes at gene promoters in eukaryotes.
source: a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) of about 140 bp in length is flanked by two well-positioned nucleosomes, one of which, the +1 nucleosome, sits on the transcription start site (TSS)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations (Bernstein et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2009; Yuan et al., 2005).

claim: The +1 nucleosome is enriched for the noncanonical histone variant H2A.Z.
source: The +1 nucleosome is enriched for the noncanonical histone variant H2A.Z
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Albert et al., 2007; Raisner et al., 2005).

claim: In yeast, H2A.Z is deposited into the +1 nucleosome by SWR1.
source: in yeast, H2A.Z is deposited into the +1 nucleosome by SWR1 (Swi2/Snf2-related ATPase complex), a chromatin remodeler in the INO80 family of remodelers
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations (Korber and Hörz, 2004; Krogan et al., 2004; Mizuguchi et al., 2004; Ranjan et al., 2013).

claim: The insertion of H2A.Z into the +1 nucleosome is highly conserved and plays an important role in regulating transcription.
source: The insertion of H2A.Z into the +1 nucleosome is highly conserved and plays an important role in regulating transcription
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Giaimo et al., 2019; Rudnizky et al., 2016).

claim: The affinity of SWR1 for nucleosomes is enhanced by both long-linker DNA and histone acetylation.
source: The affinity of SWR1 for nucleosomes is enhanced by both long-linker DNA (Ranjan et al., 2013; Yen et al., 2013) and histone acetylation (Zhang et al., 2005)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SWR1 predominantly deposits H2A.Z on the long-linker distal face of the nucleosome.
source: A recent single-molecule study further showed that SWR1 likely exploits preferential interactions with long-linker length DNA by demonstrating that H2A.Z is predominantly deposited on the long-linker distal face of the nucleosome (Poyton et al., 2022), similar to what is observed in vivo (Rhee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited single-molecule study.

claim: Facilitated diffusion has been shown to be essential for expediting the rate at which transcription factors and other DNA-binding proteins can bind their target compared to a 3D search alone.
source: Facilitated diffusion has been shown to be essential for expediting the rate at which transcription factors and other DNA-binding proteins can bind their target compared to a 3D search alone
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations (Berg et al., 1981; Elf et al., 2007; Hannon et al., 1986; Ricchetti et al., 1988; von Hippel and Berg, 1989).

claim: In vivo single-particle tracking found that chromatin remodelers have bound-state diffusion coefficients that are larger than that of bound H2B.
source: Recently published in vivo single-particle tracking found that chromatin remodelers have bound-state diffusion coefficients that are larger than that of bound H2B
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vivo studies (Kim et al., 2021; Ranjan et al., 2020).

claim: SWR1's core ATPase is a superfamily 2 (SF2) double-stranded DNA translocase.
source: SWR1's core ATPase, like other chromatin remodelers, is a superfamily 2 (SF2) double-stranded DNA translocase
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Nodelman and Bowman, 2021; Yan and Chen, 2020).

claim: The on-rate for SWR1 binding to 20 bp DNA was 1 × 10⁶ M⁻¹ s⁻¹.
source: The on-rate for SWR1 binding to 20 bp DNA, the approximate size of linker DNA between intragenic nucleosomes in yeast, was 1 × 106 M−1 s−1.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: Increasing the DNA length to 150 bp significantly increased the SWR1 binding rate 36-fold to 3.6 × 10⁷ M⁻¹ s⁻¹.
source: Increasing the DNA length to 150 bp, the approximate size of the NDR in yeast, significantly increased the binding rate 36-fold to 3.6 × 107 M−1 s−1.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: kbind for SWR1 increased linearly with DNA length between 20 bp and 150 bp.
source: kbind increased linearly with DNA length between these two values (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Longer DNA substrates may harbor more potential SWR1-binding sites.
source: This result suggests that longer DNA substrates may harbor more potential SWR1-binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the linear relationship between DNA length and binding rate.

claim: Longer DNA molecules could accommodate multiple bound SWR1 molecules.
source: In support of this, we found that longer DNA molecules could accommodate multiple bound SWR1 molecules, with the likelihood of multiple binding events increasing with DNA length
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The lifetime of SWR1 bound to 20 bp DNA (tbound) was 1.5 ± 0.3 s.
source: Whereas tbound for 20 bp DNA was 1.5 ± 0.3 s
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: tbound for SWR1 binding to 40 and 60 bp DNA increased to 9 ± 1.4 and 12 ± 5.8 s, respectively.
source: tbound for SWR1 binding to 40 and 60 bp DNA increased to 9 ± 1.4 and 12 ± 5.8 s, respectively
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: Once the DNA was 80 bp or longer, the lifetime of SWR1 binding increased dramatically to at least 30 s, the photobleaching limit of the measurement.
source: Once the DNA was 80 bp or longer, however, the lifetime increased dramatically to at least 30 s, the photobleaching limit of our measurement
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SWR1 remained bound to 150 bp DNA with a lifetime of approximately 3 min at lower laser power.
source: Measurements at lower laser power showed that SWR1 remained bound to 150 bp DNA with a life time of approximately 3 min
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: tbound was unchanged in the presence of ATP but was sensitive to ionic strength, decreasing with added salt.
source: tbound was unchanged in the presence of ATP but was sensitive to ionic strength, decreasing with added salt
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: tbound decreased in the presence of competitor DNA.
source: Curiously, tbound also decreased in the presence of competitor DNA
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: The affinity of SWR1 for DNA greater than 60 bp is primarily limited by the on-rate.
source: The kinetic measurements presented here show that the affinity of SWR1 for DNA greater than 60 bp is primarily limited by the on-rate
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that on-rate increases more dramatically than off-rate with DNA length.

claim: The increased occupancy of SWR1 at longer NDRs observed in yeast is a result of the increased probability of SWR1 finding the NDR, as opposed to an increase in the residence time of SWR1.
source: suggesting the increased occupancy of SWR1 at longer NDRs observed in yeast (Ranjan et al., 2013) is a result of the increased probability of SWR1 finding the NDR, as opposed to an increase in the residence time of SWR1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data and cited in vivo observations.

claim: Cy3-SWR1 bound to lambda DNA is mobile.
source: Cy3-SWR1 bound to lambda DNA is mobile, demonstrating that Cy3-SWR1 can move on DNA once bound
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: The movement of SWR1 on DNA did not appear to be unidirectional.
source: the movement did not appear to be unidirectional
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and MSD analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The initial portion of the MSD versus time curve for SWR1 is linear, suggesting that diffusion is Brownian.
source: Therefore, we plotted mean square displacement (MSD) versus time and found that the initial portion of the curve is linear, suggesting that diffusion is Brownian
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The diffusion coefficient observed (D1,obs) for Cy3-SWR1 was 0.013 ± 0.002 μm²/s in buffer alone.
source: The diffusion coefficient observed (D1,obs) for Cy3-SWR1 was 0.013 ± 0.002 μm2/s in buffer alone
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 2E, F.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of SWR1 is comparable to other proteins with characterized 1D diffusion.
source: This diffusion coefficient is comparable to other proteins with characterized 1D diffusion
evidence: This is a comparison to literature values supported by citations (Gorman et al., 2007; Park et al., 2021).

claim: D1,obs for specifically bound Cy5-dCas9 is 0.0003 ± 0.0004 μm²/s, which is 40-fold smaller than Cy3-SWR1.
source: In contrast D1,obs for specifically bound Cy5-dCas9, an immobile reference with D1,obs of 0.0003 ± 0.0004 μm2/s, is 40-fold smaller than Cy3-SWR1.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data used as a control for immobility.

claim: SWR1 undergoes Brownian diffusion on nucleosome-free DNA.
source: These measurements clearly show that SWR1 undergoes Brownian diffusion on nucleosome-free DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from Figure 2.

claim: The MSDs of Cy3-SWR1 in the presence of ATP remained linear, showing that SWR1 does not translocate directionally on DNA.
source: The MSDs of Cy3-SWR1 in the presence of ATP remained linear, showing that SWR1 does not translocate directionally on DNA
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The increased slope of the MSDs in the ATP condition indicates that ATP increases the diffusion of SWR1.
source: The increased slope of the MSDs in the ATP condition, however, does indicate that ATP increases the diffusion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SWR1 diffuses a greater distance from the starting position in the presence of ATP and its motion is not directional.
source: An overlay of all trajectories from both conditions further demonstrates that SWR1 diffuses a greater distance from the starting position in the presence of ATP and that its motion is not directional
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The distribution in diffusion coefficients in the presence of ATP and ATPγS are both shifted to higher values compared to in the absence of ATP or in the presence of ADP.
source: The distribution in diffusion coefficients in the presence of ATP and ATPγS are both shifted to higher values compared to in the absence of ATP or in the presence of ADP
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SWR1 diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ATP (D1,obs = 0.024 μm²/s ± 0.001) was not significantly different than diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ATPγS (D1,obs = 0.026 μm²/s ± 0.002).
source: SWR1 diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ATP (D1,obs = 0.024 μm2/s ± 0.001) was not significantly different than diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ATPγS (D1,obs = 0.026 μm2/s ± 0.002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SWR1 diffusion in the absence of ATP (D1,obs = 0.013 μm²/s ± 0.002) was not different than SWR1 diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ADP (D1,obs = 0.011 μm²/s ± 0.002).
source: Similarly, SWR1 diffusion in the absence of ATP (D1,obs = 0.013 μm2/s ± 0.002) was not different than SWR1 diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ADP (D1,obs = 0.011 μm2/s ± 0.002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ATP decreased the fraction of slow or immobile Cy3-SWR1 molecules.
source: Additionally, we found that ATP decreased the fraction of slow or immobile Cy3-SWR1 molecules, defined as those molecules that show D1 values that are indistinguishable from dCas9 values
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 9% of Cy3-SWR1 were slow or immobile in the presence of ATP, while 32% were slow or immobile in buffer alone.
source: While 9% of Cy3-SWR1 were slow or immobile in the presence of ATP, 32% were slow or immobile in buffer alone.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: While SWR1 does not actively translocate on DNA, binding of ATP increases the mobility of SWR1 on DNA.
source: These results show that while SWR1 does not actively translocate on DNA, binding of ATP increases the mobility of SWR1 on DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from Figure 3.

claim: SWR1 binding to DNA is mediated in part by the Swc2 subunit, which harbors a positively charged and unstructured DNA-binding domain (DBD).
source: SWR1 binding to DNA is mediated in part by the Swc2 subunit, which harbors a positively charged and unstructured DNA-binding domain (DBD)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Ranjan et al., 2013).

claim: Swc2 DBD also diffuses on DNA.
source: We found that Swc2 also diffuses on DNA
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The median diffusion coefficient of Swc2 DBD (D1,obs = 1.04 μm²/s ± 0.09) was approximately 40-fold larger than that of SWR1 in the presence of 1 mM ATP.
source: however the median diffusion coefficient, D1,obs = 1.04 μm2/s ± 0.09, was approximately 40-fold larger than that of SWR1 in the presence of 1 mM ATP
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The scaling relationship between size and diffusion coefficient is consistent with SWR1 and Swc2 DBD utilizing rotationally coupled sliding.
source: Based on theoretical models of rotation-coupled versus -uncoupled diffusion, the scaling relationship between size and diffusion coefficient is consistent with SWR1 and Swc2 DBD utilizing rotationally coupled sliding
evidence: This is an inference based on theoretical models and experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both SWR1 and Swc2 DBD show increased diffusion with increasing concentrations of potassium chloride.
source: Next, we found that both SWR1 and Swc2 DBD show increased diffusion with increasing concentrations of potassium chloride
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both SWR1 and Swc2 DBD showed decreasing binding lifetimes with increasing salt.
source: and each showed decreasing binding lifetimes with increasing salt
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both increased diffusion and decreased binding lifetimes are features of 1D hopping.
source: Both increased diffusion and decreased binding lifetimes are features of 1D hopping, as the more time a protein spends in microscopic dissociation and reassociation the faster it can move on DNA, but also falls off DNA more frequently
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Bonnet et al., 2008; Mirny et al., 2009).

claim: Swc2 DBD experienced shortened dwell-times in the presence of competitor DNA.
source: Like SWR1, Swc2 DBD experienced shortened dwell-times in the presence of competitor DNA
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The median diffusion of SWR1 is below the upper limit with rotation in all conditions measured.
source: In all conditions measured, the median diffusion of SWR1 is below the upper limit with rotation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and theoretical calculations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Some individual traces have diffusion coefficients that surpass the theoretical maximum with rotation, indicating that there may be alternative modes for engaging with DNA.
source: Nonetheless, some individual traces have diffusion coefficients that surpass this theoretical maximum, indicating that there may be alternative modes for engaging with DNA (e.g., infrequent hopping), which allows it to surpass the upper limit with rotation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and citations (Ahmadi et al., 2018; Gorman et al., 2010).

claim: Swc2 DBD exhibited median diffusion coefficients below the theoretical maximum with rotation, with some traces having diffusion coefficients above this limit.
source: A similar phenomenon was observed for Swc2 DBD, which also exhibited median diffusion coefficients below the theoretical maximum with rotation, with some traces having diffusion coefficients above this limit
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SWR1 utilizes a majority 1D helically coupled sliding with occasional hopping (or monkey bar-like movements) to diffuse on DNA.
source: These trends are consistent with a model in which SWR1 utilizes a majority 1D helically coupled sliding with occasional hopping (or monkey bar-like movements) to diffuse on DNA
evidence: This is a model inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in Figure 4 and illustrated in Figure 4D.

claim: Out of 106 traces with colocalization events between SWR1 and dCas9, 67% showed SWR1 moving away from dCas9 toward where it came from as if it was reflected from a boundary.
source: Out of 106 traces with colocalization events, 67% showed SWR1 moving away from dCas9 toward where it came from as if it was reflected from a boundary
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 5B, C.

claim: 30% of traces showed SWR1 immobile and colocalized with dCas9 for the duration of the trace.
source: Another 30% of traces showed SWR1 immobile and colocalized with dCas9 for the duration of the trace, which we describe as stuck
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 5C, D.

claim: Only 3% of all colocalization events exhibited a crossover event where SWR1 bypassed dCas9.
source: Only 3% of all colocalization events exhibited a crossover event
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 5C, E.

claim: The ability of dCas9 to block SWR1 diffusion in most encounters further supports a model in which SWR1 mainly engages in helically coupled sliding.
source: The ability of dCas9 to block SWR1 diffusion in most encounters further supports a model in which SWR1 mainly engages in helically coupled sliding
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from Figure 5.

claim: On average, 40 ± 5 nucleosomes were incorporated onto the lambda nucleosome arrays.
source: On average, 40 ± 5 nucleosomes were incorporated onto the lambda nucleosome arrays as shown by nucleosome unwrapping force–distance curves
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 6B–E.

claim: Nucleosomes showed detectable unwrapping at forces 15 pN or greater.
source: nucleosomes showed detectable unwrapping at forces 15 pN or greater
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and citations (Brower-Toland et al., 2002; Fierz and Poirier, 2019).

claim: Each nucleosome unwrapping event resulted in a characteristic lengthening of the array by ~25 nm.
source: with a characteristic lengthening of the array by ~25 nm with each unwrapping event
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and citation (Spakman et al., 2020).

claim: The behavior of SWR1 on lambda nucleosome arrays was notably different than on naked lambda DNA.
source: Overall, the behavior of SWR1 on lambda nucleosome arrays was notably different than on naked lambda DNA
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F, G.

claim: The mean MSD for SWR1 on naked DNA increases linearly at short time scales (<2 s), whereas the mean MSD for SWR1 on the lambda nucleosome array plateaus over this same time scale, indicative of confined 1D diffusion.
source: The mean MSD for SWR1 on naked DNA increases linearly at short time scales (<2 s), whereas the mean MSD for SWR1 on the lambda nucleosome array plateaus over this same time scale, indicative of confined 1D diffusion
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: SWR1 on naked DNA has an α = 0.88 over a 2-s time scale, whereas SWR1 on the lambda array has an α = 0.24 reflecting considerable confinement.
source: Whereas SWR1 on naked DNA has an α = 0.88 over a 2-s time scale, SWR1 on the lambda array has an α = 0.24 reflecting considerable confinement.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data analysis.

claim: The mean MSD appears to approach a limit of 0.054 μm² for SWR1 on nucleosome arrays.
source: By fitting the MSD curve to an exponential function, the mean MSD appears to approach a limit of 0.054 μm2
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The mean distance between nucleosomes is equal to 0.35 μm assuming an even distribution of an average of 40 nucleosomes per array.
source: Assuming an even distribution of an average of 40 nucleosomes per array (Figure 6E), the mean distance between nucleosomes is equal to 0.35 μm
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data.

claim: The length of DNA to which SWR1 diffusion is confined is approximately 0.23 μm.
source: whereas the length of DNA to which SWR1 diffusion is confined is approximately 0.23 μm, determined from the square root of the MSD limit described above.
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data.

claim: SWR1 diffusion is confined to the space between nucleosomes.
source: These data, therefore, suggest that SWR1 diffusion is confined to the space between nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from Figure 6.

claim: The overall percentages within individual trajectories spent in the immobile state is drastically increased for nucleosome arrays.
source: we did observe that the overall percentages within individual trajectories spent in the immobile state is drastically increased for nucleosome arrays
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: SWR1 spends more time immobile on the nucleosome array as compared to on naked DNA.
source: a dwell-time analysis of the SWR1 immobile state within trajectories (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F) shows that SWR1 spends more time immobile on the nucleosome array as compared to on naked DNA
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F.

claim: SWR1 diffusion on DNA is confined by nucleosomes and may result in transient nucleosomal interactions.
source: In summary, SWR1 diffusion on DNA is confined by nucleosomes and may result in transient nucleosomal interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from Figure 6 and supplementary figures.

claim: Approximately 47% of SWR1 molecules are bound to chromatin and the remainder is performing 3D diffusion in vivo.
source: Single-particle tracking in vivo has shown that approximately 47% of SWR1 molecules are bound to chromatin and the remainder is performing 3D diffusion
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Ranjan et al., 2020).

claim: SWR1 would require 46 ms to scan and encounter a flanking nucleosome by 1D diffusion at 0.024 μm²/s from the center of an average NDR of ~150 bp.
source: Once bound (e.g., near the center of an average NDR of ~150 bp) our findings suggest that SWR1 would require 46 ms (see Materials and methods) to scan and encounter a flanking nucleosome by 1D diffusion at 0.024 μm2/s.
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental diffusion coefficient data.

claim: SWR1 bound to chromatin has a bound-state diffusion coefficient that is ~twofold larger than the diffusion of chromatin itself (SWR1 D bound 0.063 ± 0.0003 μm²/s versus histone H2B D bound 0.028 ± 0.0002 μm²/s).
source: SWR1 bound to chromatin has been shown to have a bound-state diffusion coefficient that is ~twofold larger than the diffusion of chromatin itself (SWR1 D bound 0.063 ± 0.0003 μm2/s versus histone H2B D bound 0.028 ± 0.0002 μm2/s)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Ranjan et al., 2020).

claim: Other yeast chromatin remodelers that act on nucleosomes adjacent to the NDR (RSC, SWI/SNF, ISW2, and INO80) are similarly more diffusive than histone H2B in their chromatin-bound states.
source: A later study found that other yeast chromatin remodelers that act on nucleosomes adjacent to the NDR (RSC, SWI/SNF, ISW2, and INO80) are similarly more diffusive than histone H2B in their chromatin-bound states
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Kim et al., 2021).

claim: These chromatin remodelers are dependent on the ability of their ATPase domains to bind or hydrolyze ATP in order to exhibit enhanced bound diffusion.
source: and are, similar to SWR1, dependent on the ability of their ATPase domains to bind or hydrolyze ATP in order to exhibit this enhanced bound diffusion
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Kim et al., 2021).

claim: When complexed with a canonical nucleosome and the H2A.Z–H2B dimer, SWR1 can rapidly perform the ATP hydrolysis-dependent histone exchange reaction on average in 2.4 s.
source: A single-molecule TIRF study on the molecular mechanism of the SWR1 histone exchange reaction recently reported that when complexed with a canonical nucleosome and the H2A.Z–H2B dimer, SWR1 can rapidly perform the ATP hydrolysis-dependent histone exchange reaction on average in 2.4 s
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Poyton et al., 2022).

claim: The SWR1-catalyzed histone H2A.Z exchange on chromatin may be an intrinsically rapid event that occurs on a time scale of seconds.
source: The SWR1-catalyzed histone H2A.Z exchange on chromatin may therefore be an intrinsically rapid event that occurs on a time scale of seconds.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited experimental data.

claim: The fluorescently labeled SWR1 complex maintains full histone exchange activity.
source: We demonstrated that the fluorescently labeled SWR1 complex maintains full histone exchange activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cy3-labeled Swc7 comigrated with the rest of the SWR1 subunits, demonstrating incorporation of Swc7 back into the SWR1 complex.
source: Subsequent purification on a glycerol gradient revealed that the Cy3-labeled Swc7 comigrated with the rest of the SWR1 subunits, demonstrating incorporation of Swc7 back into the SWR1 complex
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The histone exchange activity of the labeled Cy3-SWR1 was identical to that of wild-type SWR1.
source: The histone exchange activity of the labeled Cy3-SWR1 was identical to that of wild-type SWR1 as revealed by an electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cy3-Swc7 alone exhibited no affinity for 150 bp DNA.
source: Cy3-Swc7 alone exhibited no affinity for 150 bp DNA (data not shown)
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The observed fluorescent spots represent the Cy3–SWR1 complex as Cy3-Swc7 alone was unable to bind DNA.
source: The observed fluorescent spots represent the Cy3–SWR1 complex as Cy3-Swc7 alone was unable to bind DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SWR1 requires ATP to perform the histone exchange reaction.
source: SWR1 requires ATP to perform the histone exchange reaction
evidence: This is established knowledge about SWR1 function.

claim: Basal levels of ATP hydrolysis when any one of the required substrates for the histone exchange reaction is missing is low.
source: and basal levels of ATP hydrolysis when any one of the required substrates for the histone exchange reaction is missing is low
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Luk et al., 2010).

claim: The core ATPase domain of SWR1, Swr1, belongs to the SF2 of translocases which have two lobes that switch between an open and closed conformation with ATP binding and hydrolysis.
source: The core ATPase domain of SWR1, Swr1, like other chromatin remodelers, belongs to the SF2 of translocases which have two lobes that switch between an open and closed conformation with ATP binding and hydrolysis
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Beyer et al., 2013; Nodelman et al., 2020).

claim: Swc2 forms an extended interface with the core ATPase.
source: In the present study, we further investigated a DNA-binding subunit, Swc2, which forms an extended interface with the core ATPase
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Willhoft et al., 2018).

claim: Proteins that hop on DNA have increased diffusion with increased monovalent cation concentration.
source: Proteins that hop on DNA therefore have increased diffusion with increased monovalent cation concentration, as a higher screening potential results in more frequent hops.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein-DNA interactions.

claim: Proteins that utilize sliding as the predominant form of 1D diffusion cannot bypass proteins or nucleosomes.
source: Other studies have found that proteins that utilize sliding as the predominant form of 1D diffusion cannot bypass proteins or nucleosomes
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Brown et al., 2016; Gorman et al., 2010; Hedglin and O'Brien, 2010).

claim: A protein that predominantly hops may be able to bypass obstacles such as proteins or nucleosomes.
source: whereas a protein that predominantly hops may be able to bypass these obstacles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein diffusion mechanisms.

claim: The utilization of hopping diffusion has been described as a trade-off between scanning speed and accuracy, with proven implications in target sequence bypass by the transcription factor LacI.
source: The utilization of hopping diffusion has been described as a trade-off between scanning speed and accuracy, with proven implications in target sequence bypass by the transcription factor LacI
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Marklund et al., 2020).

claim: In the yeast genome, there are approximately 61,568 annotated nucleosomes.
source: In the yeast genome, there are approximately 61,568 annotated nucleosomes
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Jiang and Pugh, 2009; Kubik et al., 2015).

claim: 4576 nucleosomes are identified as potential +1 nucleosomes enriched in H2A.Z.
source: of which 4576 are identified as potential +1 nucleosomes enriched in H2A.Z
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Tramantano et al., 2016).

claim: Only 7% of nucleosomes are targets of SWR1 histone exchange.
source: Since only 7% of nucleosomes are targets of SWR1
evidence: This is a calculation based on cited data (4576/61568 ≈ 7%).

claim: +1 nucleosomes use their adjacent NDRs as antennas, promoting SWR1 binding and 1D search to encounter flanking nucleosomes.
source: we believe that +1 nucleosomes use their adjacent NDRs as antennas, promoting SWR1 binding and 1D search to encounter flanking nucleosomes
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings and supported by citation (Mirny et al., 2009).

claim: 1D diffusion may be an important aspect of target search for chromatin remodelers that act on nucleosomes adjacent to the NDR, such as RSC, SWI/SNF, ISW2, and INO80.
source: 1D diffusion at NDRs may be an important aspect of SWR1 target search and potentially a common feature for chromatin remodelers that acts upon nucleosomes adjacent to the NDR.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings for SWR1 and cited in vivo data (Kim et al., 2021).

claim: Acetylation of the +1 nucleosome may help establish the directionality of the interaction when assessing the two NDR-flanking nucleosomes.
source: While there is evidence that acetylation of the +1 nucleosome may help establish the directionality of the interaction when assessing the two NDR-flanking nucleosomes
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Ranjan et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: Even nucleosomes lacking acetylation can reduce the diffusion of the SWR1 complex possibly through nucleosome engagement.
source: data from our study indicate that even nucleosomes lacking acetylation can reduce the diffusion of the SWR1 complex possibly through nucleosome engagement.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from Figure 6.

claim: H2A.Z is preferentially enriched at inactive promoters.
source: Additionally, H2A.Z is preferentially enriched at inactive promoters
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Li et al., 2005).

claim: Promoter NDR regions from yeast are highly rigid and this unique property helps instruct the chromatin remodeler, INO80, to position nucleosomes at the boundary of the rigid NDR.
source: A sequencing study discovering the intrinsic flexibility of different DNA sequences helped establish that promoter NDR regions from yeast are highly rigid and this unique property compared to gene-body DNA helps instruct the chromatin remodeler, INO80, a close relative of SWR1, to position nucleosomes at the boundary of the rigid NDR helping to establish the defined positioning of the +1 nucleosome
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Basu et al., 2021).

claim: In vivo binding of SWR1 has been shown to be reduced by fragile nucleosome occupancy of NDRs.
source: In vivo binding of SWR1, as shown via ChIP-seq, has already been shown to be reduced by fragile nucleosome occupancy of NDRs
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Ranjan et al., 2013; Venters and Pugh, 2009).

claim: The localization precision of the measurement is approximately 82 nm.
source: This results in a σ = 82 nm.
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental parameters using a standard formula.

claim: Lambda DNA tethered at 5 pN tension resulted in a length approximately 92% of its contour length (15.2 µm).
source: Lambda DNA tethered at its ends to two optically trapped beads was pulled to a tension of 5 pN, which resulted in a length approximately 92% of its contour length (15.2 µm).
evidence: This is an experimental observation based on optical tweezers measurements.

claim: The length per basepair of DNA at 5 pN tension is 0.31 nm.
source: The length per basepair of DNA, 0.31 nm, is therefore slightly shorter than the value at full contour length
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data and supported by citation (Baumann et al., 2000).

claim: The length of the NDR (150 bp) in the experimental conditions is approximately 0.047 µm long.
source: The length of the NDR, 150 bp, in our conditions is therefore roughly 0.047 µm long.
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental parameters.

claim: The time required to scan 150 bp of DNA is approximately 0.093 s (93 ms) assuming a continuous model with a diffusion coefficient of 0.024 µm²/s.
source: we can approximate the time required to scan this length of DNA to be 0.093 s assuming a continuous model
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured diffusion coefficient and the one-dimensional diffusion equation, supported by citation (Berg, 1983).
